obtained.how: Michigan DNR's own copy of the report (Fisheries Research Report 1992, 33-page scanned PDF with a text layer) on the DNR fisheries library server

bibliography.checked_against: the report's cover and title page (PDF pp. 1-3)
bibliography.corrections: cover and title page read 'Overwinter Consumption of Bluegills by Walleye and Yellow Perch' (the abstract page has 'Bluegill'); Fisheries Research Report 1992, dated April 20, 1997 (the abstract page's header reads 'No. 1992, 1996'); Michigan Department of Natural Resources, Fisheries Division (Institute for Fisheries Research, Ann Arbor). The paper cites it 'via Neuswanger et al. 2015': it has now been read directly, so the 'via' can go.

claims.claim: Predators raised the overwinter loss of 28-mm age-0 bluegill in Michigan ponds from 10 % to 39 %
claims.source_value: survival of age-0 bluegill 90 ± 6 % in control ponds (N = 7) vs 61 ± 16 % in ponds with predators (N = 9) over the four winters 1989-90 to 1992-93, i.e. losses of 10 % and 39 %; bluegill averaged 28 mm TL and 0.24 g at stocking in most years
claims.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 9), Results; abstract p. 1 (PDF p. 3); p. 5 (PDF p. 7) for the 28 mm
claims.quote: overwinter survival of age-0 bluegill in the ponds with predators was 61±16% compared to 90±6%
claims.conditions: 0.2-ha experimental ponds at the Saline Fisheries Research Station, Michigan; ice-covered, ~4 °C, December-March; predators were juvenile walleye or adult yellow perch; 1988-89 excluded (poor-condition bluegill: 19.5 % control survival, 3.1 % with predators)
claims.note: the 28 mm: 'average total length of age-0 bluegill at stocking was 28 mm' (p. 5); in 1992-93 the age-0 bluegill were 34.9 mm (Table 2 footnote)

claims.claim: and to 55 % [overwinter loss] with walleye alone
claims.source_value: 55 % is not a loss of bluegill: it is the share of total bluegill mortality attributed to predation in the walleye ponds (N = 8, range 25-89 %; 63 % for yellow perch ponds, 58 % overall). Age-0 bluegill survival in the 1991-93 walleye ponds was 47-79 % (loss 21-53 %, mean about 42 %); in 1988-89 it was 0.2-5.8 % against 12.5-24 % in the controls
claims.location: p. 8 (PDF p. 10), Results; Table 2, p. 22 (PDF p. 24); Table 4, p. 24 (PDF p. 26)
claims.quote: This percentage was similar for walleye (55%, N = 8, range: 25-89%)
claims.conditions: same ponds; partition of total mortality into predatory and non-predatory parts by the report's second method (Appendix 1)
claims.note: the preceding sentence reads 'We calculated that predators were responsible for 58% of the bluegill mortality in ponds containing predators'. A correct rewrite: 'predators accounted for 55 % of the bluegill deaths in walleye ponds'. Table 2 values read in the raw text.

claims.claim: bluegill become relatively invulnerable to pike and largemouth beyond 100-125 mm
claims.source_value: bluegill are 'relatively invulnerable to even large piscivores such as northern pike ... and largemouth bass ... after reaching a length of 100-125 mm total length'
claims.quote: relatively invulnerable to even large piscivores such as northern pike
claims.conditions: total length; an introductory statement citing Beyerle and Williams 1968 and Wahl and Stein 1988, not a result of this report
claims.note: the report adds that bluegill 'are usually not a preferred prey even at smaller sizes'. The primary sources for the threshold are Beyerle & Williams (1968) and Wahl & Stein (1988).

notes: Other useful values in the report: pond consumption of age-0 bluegill 0.38 ± 0.10 %BW/d by walleye and 0.27 ± 0.08 %BW/d by yellow perch at ~4 °C; laboratory maintenance rations at 4.4 °C of 0.075 %BW/d (adult yellow perch) and 0.32 %BW/d (small walleye); complete gastric evacuation of a 1 % bluegill meal 41 h (perch) and 77 h (walleye); December-March consumption of 3,500 and 8,600 bluegill/ha in Blueberry Pond and Cassidy Lake; age-0 bluegill can be ingested by yellow perch > 158 mm TL. Bluegill size changed little overwinter in the ponds (no size-selective loss) except where 8 of 3,400 survived.
